flashcard_questions.a: Breaking a whole market into smaller sub-groups of customers with similar wants.
Targeting customers by where they live or where the product will be used.
Statistical data relating to the population and particular groups within it.
Grouping customers by the way they lead their lives and the attitudes they share.
The money a person has left after tax has been taken off their pay.
Plotting brands on a diagram using two variables that separate them.

flashcard_questions.q: How many axes does a market map always use?
flashcard_questions.a: Two axes, such as price and quality.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a gap on a market map not guarantee success?
flashcard_questions.a: There might be no demand in that space.

flashcard_questions.q: Which luxury shoe brand sits in the premium corner of the market map?
Which outdoor brand repositioned itself as fashion through Supreme and Gucci collaborations?
Which Toyota model is priced at £57,000 for high-income enthusiasts?
What is the price of the Toyota Aygo aimed at budget-conscious buyers?
Which social class group covers skilled working-class workers such as plumbers?
What is the main benefit of segmenting a market?
flashcard_questions.a: Marketing spend focuses on the customers most likely to buy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the risk of segmenting a market too narrowly?
flashcard_questions.a: It can exclude potential customers, leaving too few to sell to.

notes: 15 cards: 6 term→definition (segmentation, location, demographics, lifestyle, disposable income, market mapping), 1 market-map structure card, 5 concept→named example with the lesson's own figures (Jimmy Choo, The North Face, Supra £57,000, Aygo £15,000, class C2), 3 single-fact benefit/risk cards. The five segmentation bases and the full A–E class ladder were not made into list cards — one class group is enough to test the idea.
